etymology: Algospeak from TikTok, c. 2020–2021. Creators who believed the platform removed or quietly suppressed videos containing kill, dead, or suicide substituted unalive (to kill, to die) and unalive myself (suicide). There were scattered jokey uses of the word before 2020, but the common sense is a moderation workaround. It spread to YouTube, true-crime and news-recap videos, and then off the screen into schools, where teachers report young children using it as an everyday word.
biblical_def: In current slang unalive means kill or die, and unalive myself means suicide. It was made to slip past the filters on TikTok and YouTube, and it has since walked off the screen into classrooms, where children say it of video-game characters, of a strict teacher, and sometimes of themselves. The Christian observation: a softer word does not make a softer thing. God’s law names it plainly: "Thou shalt not kill" (Exo 20:13), and Genesis gives the reason: "for in the image of God made he man" (Gen 9:6). That commandment guards our own lives as well as our neighbour’s: "ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body" (1Co 6:20). When the jailer at Philippi drew his sword on himself, Paul did not lecture him; he "cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here" (Act 16:28), and before morning the man was baptised and rejoicing. That is the church’s whole posture toward the despairing: a loud cry, a near presence, and Christ. "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart" (Psa 34:18), and the Lord Jesus says, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). Say this plainly to every parent: if your child uses this word about himself, even as a joke, take it seriously. Stop, ask him directly, listen, and get help that day — your pastor, your doctor, and, in the United States, the 988 crisis line or emergency services if there is any danger. A father tells his child: there is no darkness you can bring to us that will make us love you less, and no sin or sorrow too heavy for the Saviour who carried the cross. Your life is not yours to end; it is His to keep, and He keeps it gladly.
webster_summary: Gen-Z algospeak (TikTok c. 2020–present) for kill, die, or suicide, coined to dodge moderation — a softened word for what the sixth commandment forbids, and a cry from a child that must always be heard.
webster_full: UNALIVE, v.t. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; TikTok algospeak) To kill; unalive oneself, to commit suicide; unalived, killed or dead. "The main character gets unalived in the finale."
Forms: unaliving, unalive myself; common in news-recap and true-crime videos and in jokes; now heard in classrooms from young children who learned it online.
No settled older sense. A grandparent’s plain words for the same things are kill, die, and suicide — and plain words are better here.

Webster (1828), root word kill: “KILL, verb transitive 1. To deprive of life, animal or vegetable, in any manner or by any means. To kill an animal or a plant, is to put an end to the vital functions, either by destroying or essentially injuring the organs necessary to life, or by causing them to cease from action.”

Decode for parents: if your child says it about himself — even laughing — take it seriously. Ask him directly whether he has thought about ending his life, listen without panic, and get help the same day.
scriptures: For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here.
The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: Unalive softens the words for killing and self-murder so they pass the filters, and in doing so makes the gravest things sayable as jokes, even by small children.
corruption_paragraphs: Euphemism is old; men have always found gentler words for death. What is new is a euphemism made for a machine. Unalive exists because platforms flag kill and suicide, so creators invented a word the software could not read. The result is a cartoon word for the darkest act there is, small enough for a seven-year-old to say on the playground. God does not soften it: "Thou shalt not kill" (Exo 20:13), "for in the image of God made he man" (Gen 9:6). The sixth commandment forbids taking our own life as surely as our neighbour’s, for "ye are bought with a price" (1Co 6:20).

But the church must hear what is underneath the word. Many children who say it are joking; some are not, and a joke is often how a frightened child tests whether anyone will notice. Notice. Paul’s cry to the despairing jailer, "Do thyself no harm: for we are all here" (Act 16:28), is the pattern for parents: a loud voice, a near presence, and then the gospel. The Lord Jesus came for the heavy laden (Mat 11:28) and is "nigh unto them that are of a broken heart" (Psa 34:18). Teach your children the plain words, and teach them that no despair is beyond His reach. If there is danger, get help now: your pastor, your doctor, and in the United States the 988 crisis line.
roots_summary: Old English on life → alive + un- (not) → c. 2020 TikTok algospeak: unalive, to kill, to die, suicide.
roots_lines: Old English on life — in life; Middle English alive
Old English un- — not, the reverse of
Scattered jokey uses of unalive before 2020
c. 2020–2021 TikTok: unalive to dodge moderation of kill, dead, and suicide
2020s: carried off the screen into schools, used even by young children
usage: "If I fail this test my mom is going to unalive me."
Thou shalt not kill; the image of God is in every man, and in you (Exo 20:13).
Do thyself no harm: for we are all here (Act 16:28).

etymology: A blend of algorithm and -speak (the suffix of George Orwell’s Newspeak, 1949). The coded vocabulary grew on TikTok c. 2019–2021 as creators tried to keep videos from being removed or quietly suppressed by automated moderation: unalive for kill or die, SA for assault, letters swapped for numbers or symbols, and emojis standing in for words the software might flag. The name itself came into wide use through news reporting in 2022.
biblical_def: In current use algospeak is the coded vocabulary people use online to slip past automated moderation: unalive for kill, SA for assault, misspellings, swapped letters, and emojis in place of flagged words. Teens learn it without noticing, and it leaks into speech. The Christian observation: coded speech is as old as Gilead, where one word, Shibboleth, sorted friend from foe at the passages of Jordan (Jdg 12:6). Sometimes code is a mercy; believers under persecution have needed it. But most algospeak exists for two reasons Scripture would question. First, it softens: it gives children cute words for grave sins, and "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light" (Isa 5:20). A word that hides from a filter also hides the weight of the thing from the speaker. Second, it schools a generation in evasion, the habit of saying everything in a way that can be denied. Christ asks for the opposite: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37), and Paul, "putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour" (Eph 4:25). And nothing is truly coded before God: "whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light" (Luk 12:3). A father tells his children: learn the code so you can understand your friends, then speak plainly. Call sin by its name and grief by its name, because a thing named rightly can be brought to Christ.
webster_summary: Gen-Z coinage (algorithm + -speak, c. 2021–present) for the coded online vocabulary that dodges platform moderation — a schooling in softened, deniable speech that Scripture answers with yea, nay, and the light.
webster_full: ALGOSPEAK, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2021–present; from algorithm + -speak) Coded words, misspellings, and emoji substitutions used online to avoid automated moderation or suppression. "She said unalive because that’s the algospeak for it."
Common examples: unalive (kill, die), SA (assault), spicy (indecent), letters swapped for numbers or symbols, and emojis in place of flagged words.
Older relatives: thieves’ cant, rhyming slang, and the euphemisms every age invents for death and disease.

Webster (1828), root word cant: “CANT, noun 1. A toss; a throw, thrust or push with a sudden jerk; as, to give a ball a cant […] 2. A whining, singing manner of speech; a quaint, affected mode of uttering words either in conversation or preaching. 3. The whining speech of beggars, as in asking alms and making complaints of their distresses. 4.”
Decode for parents: when your child uses a cute word for a grave thing, ask what it stands for; the code may be hiding something he needs to say plainly.
scriptures: Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right. Then they took him, and slew him at the passages of Jordan: and there fell at that time of the Ephraimites forty and two thousand.
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops.
corruption_summary: Algospeak trains a generation to soften grave things and to say everything deniably, the reverse of the plain, truthful speech Christ commands.
corruption_paragraphs: There is honest cleverness in it, and a code is not sin by itself. The Shibboleth of Gilead was a code (Jdg 12:6), and persecuted believers have long spoken in signs. But algospeak’s chief work is softening. It invents baby words for death, assault, and self-murder so they can be posted beside dance videos, and the softening does not stay on the platform. Isaiah’s woe falls on those who "put darkness for light" (Isa 5:20); a word built to hide a thing from a filter ends by hiding its weight from the heart.

Its second work is evasion. A child fluent in algospeak learns that the skill of speech is to say what you mean in a way no one can pin on you. Scripture wants the reverse: "Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37), "speak every man truth with his neighbour" (Eph 4:25). And no code fools God; what is "spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light" (Luk 12:3). Teach your children to understand the code and to outgrow it: plain words for sin, plain words for sorrow, and the plain name of Jesus Christ.
roots_summary: Algorithm (from the name of al-Khwarizmi) + Orwell’s Newspeak (1949) → c. 2021–2022 algospeak, code words that dodge moderation.
roots_lines: Arabic al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-c. mathematician → Medieval Latin algorismus → English algorithm
George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949): Newspeak, and the suffix -speak
c. 2019–2021 TikTok: coded words to avoid removal and suppression
2022: algospeak enters wide use through news reporting
Now: code words carried from the screen into speech
usage: "You can’t say that word in your video, use the algospeak version."
Call evil by its name; woe to the softened word (Isa 5:20).
No code is hidden from God (Luk 12:3).

etymology: Older than TikTok: moderators of early internet forums in the 2000s (the Something Awful forums are the usual citation) used a shadow ban to let a troublemaker keep posting while no one else could see his posts. The word broke into general use c. 2018, when users of Twitter, Instagram, and later TikTok accused the platforms of quietly limiting their reach. Platforms rarely admit it, and the word now covers any unexplained drop in views.
biblical_def: In current slang to be shadowbanned is to be quietly suppressed by a platform: you can still post, but your videos stop appearing on anyone’s feed, and no one tells you why. Creators blame it for every bad week, and teens fear it the way an earlier generation feared being left out. The Christian observation: the shadowban is a picture of a world where reach is everything and a hidden hand decides it. Scripture moves both the fear and the hand. Reach was never the measure of a life; John the Baptist, watching his crowds drain away to Jesus, said, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Joh 3:30). The hidden hand behind every outcome is not a company but the Lord: "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33). And the best work of a Christian is meant to go unseen by men: "pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly" (Mat 6:6). No platform can shadowban God’s truth. Paul wrote from a prison cell, "the word of God is not bound" (2Ti 2:9), and God says of His word, "it shall not return unto me void" (Isa 55:11). Real suppression of Christian speech happens and should be named; but anxiety about views is a different thing and needs a different cure. A father tells his son: if your views drop, your worth has not. Post what is true and good, and leave the reach to God; the Father who sees in secret is the only audience whose reward lasts.
webster_summary: Internet slang (2000s forum moderation; mainstream c. 2018–present) for silent suppression of a user’s reach — a fear of invisibility that Scripture answers with the Father who sees in secret and a word that is not bound.
webster_full: SHADOWBAN, n. / v.t. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2018–present; from 2000s forum moderation) The silent restriction of a user’s posts so that few or none see them, without notice. "My views fell off a cliff. I think I got shadowbanned."
Shadowbanned, adj.; also shadow ban, ghost ban, stealth ban. Often blamed, rightly or wrongly, for any drop in engagement.
Older relatives: being blackballed, sent to Coventry, or quietly left off the list — exclusion without explanation.
Webster (1828), root word ban: “BAN, noun 1. A public proclamation or edict; a public order or notice, mandatory or prohibitory. In a more particular sense, 2.”
Decode for parents: a teen who talks about being shadowbanned is often measuring himself by his views; help him find a better measure.
scriptures: He must increase, but I must decrease.
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
corruption_summary: The shadowban fear makes reach the measure of worth and a platform the hidden lord of it, where Scripture puts the disposing of all things in God’s hand and the best work in secret.
corruption_paragraphs: Hidden suppression is real. Platforms do quietly limit accounts, and Christians who speak plainly about sin have seen their reach cut; that is worth naming, and believers have always known what it is to be pushed out of the public square. But for most teens the word names something smaller and sadder: the dread that if the algorithm stops showing you, you have stopped mattering. That dread puts a company in the place of Providence. "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33).

Scripture offers a better economy. The Father "seeth in secret" (Mat 6:6), and the prayers no one sees are the ones He rewards. John the Baptist watched his audience shrink and called it joy (Joh 3:30). And the gospel itself cannot be shadowbanned: "the word of God is not bound" (2Ti 2:9). Teach your children to speak the truth whether it reaches ten or ten thousand, and to rest in the God whose word "shall not return unto me void" (Isa 55:11).
roots_summary: Old English sceadu (shade) + ban (proclamation, prohibition) → 2000s forum moderators’ shadow ban → c. 2018 social media: silent suppression of reach.
roots_lines: Old English sceadu — shade, shadow, darkness
Old English bannan — to summon, to proclaim; ban, a prohibition
2000s internet forums: shadow ban, a troublemaker left posting into the void
c. 2018: Twitter and Instagram users accuse platforms of silent limits
2020s TikTok: shadowbanned, any unexplained drop in views
usage: "Nobody’s seeing my posts, I’m literally shadowbanned."
Thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly (Mat 6:6).
The word of God is not bound (2Ti 2:9).

etymology: Abbreviation of For You page, TikTok’s main feed, which became the app’s front door after TikTok absorbed Musical.ly in 2018. Unlike older feeds built from accounts a user chose to follow, the For You page is filled by a recommendation algorithm that studies what each user watches, pauses on, and replays. Users tag posts "#fyp" in hope of landing there, and "it was on my FYP" means "the app showed it to me."
biblical_def: In current slang the FYP is TikTok’s For You page, the endless feed the app picks for each user; to say a video "came up on my FYP" is to say the algorithm chose it. Teens speak of their FYP as a kind of mirror: "my FYP knows me too well." The Christian observation: the name is the sermon. A feed built "for you" is built from your own appetites, and it learns them faster than you do. Paul warned of a time when men "after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears" (2Ti 4:3); the FYP is that heap, delivered by machine. Scripture puts the guarding of the heart on us, not on the app: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Pro 4:23). David made a vow every phone owner could copy: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3). Christ said that what we look at fills us: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Mat 6:22). And Paul gives the better curation: "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest" — "think on these things" (Php 4:8). A father tells his son: the FYP is not really for you; it is for the advertisers, built from your weakest moments. Train it if you must, limit it always, and spend more hours in the pages that really were written for you — the Word of God, which knows your heart better than any algorithm and loves you more.
webster_summary: Gen-Z abbreviation (TikTok, c. 2018–present) for the For You page, the algorithm-picked feed — a heap of teachers for itching ears, set against the heart Scripture tells us to keep.
webster_full: FYP, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2018–present; TikTok) For You page: the app’s main feed of videos chosen by its recommendation algorithm. "This came up on my FYP and I can’t stop watching it."
#fyp, #foryou, #foryoupage — hashtags added in hope of reaching the feed; my FYP, one’s personal feed, often spoken of as if it knew the user’s mind.
Older relatives: the newspaper front page, the evening news, the radio playlist — chosen by editors for everyone, not by a machine for one.

Webster (1828), root word page: “PAGE, noun […] One side of a leaf of a book. 1. A book or writing or writings; as the page of history. 2. Pages, in the plural, signifies also books or writings; as the sacred pages.”
Decode for parents: your child’s FYP is a map of what holds his attention; it is worth asking, gently, to see it.
scriptures: For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: The FYP serves each user a feed built from his own appetites, so that the heart is curated by a machine that profits from its weakest moments.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age had its distractions, but they came in common: the same paper, the same broadcast, the same town square. The For You page is a feed of one, assembled by studying where your thumb pauses and tuned to keep you there. It is men heaping "to themselves teachers, having itching ears" (2Ti 4:3) without even the effort of the heaping. It learns the boy’s anger, the girl’s insecurity, and the lonely night hours, and serves more of each.

Scripture never lets the eye off the hook: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3) is a vow, and vows are made by people, not by apps. "Keep thy heart with all diligence" (Pro 4:23). Teach your children that the feed is neither neutral nor their friend, that a single eye fills the body with light (Mat 6:22), and that the curation God commends is Philippians 4:8. Then set the example: put down your own phone at the table.
roots_summary: For You page → TikTok’s algorithmic main feed (2018) → #fyp, the hashtag → my FYP, one’s personal feed.
roots_lines: Latin pagina — a leaf of a book; English page
2016–2017: Douyin in China, then TikTok abroad
2018: TikTok absorbs Musical.ly; the For You page becomes its front door
#fyp: a hashtag added in hope of reaching the feed
Now: my FYP, spoken of as if it knew the user
usage: "My FYP is nothing but cooking videos and sad edits right now."
Keep thy heart; the feed will not keep it for you (Pro 4:23).
Set no wicked thing before your eyes (Psa 101:3).

etymology: POV, abbreviation of point of view, was film and fiction jargon long before the internet: a POV shot shows the scene through a character’s eyes. On TikTok c. 2019–2020 it became a genre: a caption begins "POV:" and sets a scene in the second person ("POV: you’re the new kid at lunch"), and the creator acts it out as if the viewer were inside it.
biblical_def: In current slang POV is a video format: a caption like "POV: your mom finds your report card" puts the viewer inside a little scene, and the creator plays the other part. It is often funny and sometimes surprisingly tender, and it trains a habit of imagining how a moment feels from someone else’s side. The Christian observation: taking another’s point of view is a Christian duty before it is a TikTok genre. "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others" (Php 2:4); "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). Proverbs adds a warning that many POV videos illustrate: a story told from one side always looks right. "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Pro 18:17). Many POVs cast the creator as the wronged party and the parent, teacher, or ex as the villain, and the viewer only ever sees one camera. Above all, there is one point of view that corrects every other: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD" (Isa 55:8), and "the LORD seeth not as man seeth" (1Sa 16:7). A father tells his daughter: enjoy the bit, and practise the skill — picture your friend’s side, your brother’s side, even mine. Then ask the best question of all: what does this look like from where God sits?
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (TikTok c. 2019–present, from film jargon point of view) for a second-person role-play video — a habit of imagining another’s side that Scripture commands, and a one-camera story Proverbs warns can deceive.
webster_full: POV, abbr. / n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2019–present; from film jargon) A short video in which the caption sets a scene in the second person and the creator acts it out as if the viewer were inside it. "POV: you forgot it was picture day."
Also used in plain speech to mean "picture this" or "here’s my situation": "POV: me at 2 a.m. still doing homework."
Older senses: point of view, a person’s standpoint or opinion; in film, a POV shot; in fiction, first- or third-person narration.

Webster (1828), root word view: “VIEW, noun vu. 1. Prospect; sight; reach of the eye. The walls of Pluto's palace are in view 2. The whole extent seen. Vast or extensive views present themselves to the eye. 3. Sight; power of seeing, or limit of sight. The mountain was not within our view 4. Intellectual or mental sight.”
Decode for parents: often harmless comedy; watch for the POVs that always cast parents and teachers as the villains.
scriptures: Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
corruption_summary: POV exercises a good habit, seeing from another’s side, but its one-camera stories train viewers to take every first telling as the whole truth.
corruption_paragraphs: The format has real merit. It asks a teenager to imagine being the new kid, the nervous waiter, the little sister left out, and Scripture commends that kind of imagination: "every man also on the things of others" (Php 2:4). Some of the most tender videos on any platform are POVs written by grandchildren about grandparents or by nurses about their patients.

The danger is the single camera. Many POVs are grievance pieces: the creator’s side, perfectly lit, with the parent or teacher or friend reduced to a caricature. Proverbs saw it coming: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Pro 18:17). Teach your children to ask for the other side before they take a side, and to remember that only one point of view sees everything: "my thoughts are not your thoughts" (Isa 55:8).
roots_summary: Latin videre (to see) → point of view, a standpoint → film POV shot → c. 2019 TikTok: POV:, the second-person role-play video.
roots_lines: Latin punctum (a point) and videre (to see)
18th c. English point of view — the standpoint from which a thing is seen
20th c. film and fiction: the POV shot, narration through a character’s eyes
c. 2019–2020 TikTok: "POV:" captions and acted scenes
Now: "POV" as everyday shorthand for "picture this"
usage: "POV: you’re the only one who did the reading."
Look on the things of others, not only your own (Php 2:4).
The first story always sounds right; wait for the second (Pro 18:17).

etymology: From story time, the read-aloud hour in libraries and classrooms since the early 20th century. On YouTube in the 2010s "storytime" became a video genre: a creator, often while doing her makeup or eating, narrates a dramatic personal anecdote ("STORYTIME: my roommate stole my identity"). TikTok compressed it into one-minute and multi-part versions c. 2020, and the word now marks any narrated real-life tale online.
biblical_def: In current slang a storytime is a video in which someone narrates a true (or true-ish) personal anecdote: the worst date, the wild boss, the family drama, often in parts, often while doing something else. The best are funny; many are other people’s secrets told to strangers. The Christian observation: God made us storytellers and commands the telling. "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD" (Psa 78:4). Israel’s fathers were to talk of God’s works "when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way" (Deu 6:7). When Jesus delivered the man of the Gadarenes, He sent him home with one task: "tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee" (Mar 5:19) — a storytime with a commission. But the genre has a shadow. Much of it is the talebearer’s trade: a roommate, a friend, an ex, a parent laid bare for views, and "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter" (Pro 11:13). Embellishment is part of the craft, and the truth is not served by it. Paul sets the test for every story: "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29). A father tells his son: tell your stories — tell them well, tell them true, and tell the best one often, the story of what the Lord has done for you. But if a story is someone else’s shame, it is not yours to tell.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (YouTube 2010s, TikTok c. 2020–present, from the library story time) for a narrated personal-anecdote video — a gift of telling Scripture commands, too often spent on other people’s secrets.
webster_full: STORYTIME, n. (Gen-Z slang, 2010s–present; YouTube and TikTok) A video in which the creator narrates a dramatic or funny personal anecdote, often in several parts. "Storytime: how I got kicked out of the library."
Often paired with another activity (makeup, cooking, driving); part 2, part 3 for serial tellings; storytime as a caption tag.
Older sense: story time, the hour when a librarian, teacher, or parent reads aloud to children.

Webster (1828), root word story: “STORY, noun […] 1. A verbal narration or recital of a series of facts or incidents. WE observe in children a strong passion for hearing stories. 2. A written narrative of a series of facts or events. There is probably on record no story more interesting than that of Joseph in Genesis. 3. History;”
Decode for parents: ask whose story is being told; your child’s friends, siblings, and you are all possible characters.
scriptures: We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
corruption_summary: Storytime turns the God-given gift of telling into a trade in other people’s secrets and in drama polished for views.
corruption_paragraphs: A people who forget their stories forget their God, and Scripture is mostly story. Psalm 78 is a father’s storytime, told so the children "might set their hope in God" (Psa 78:7). A family that tells its stories at the table, including the stories of answered prayer, is obeying Deuteronomy 6:7, and a teenager who can hold a room with a well-told tale has a gift worth sharpening.

The online genre bends the gift. A storytime earns views by drama, and drama is usually someone else’s: the roommate’s meltdown, the friend’s betrayal, the parents’ divorce. The talebearer has always had an audience (Pro 11:13); now he has millions. And the craft rewards stretching the truth a little further each part. Teach your children Paul’s test, "that it may minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29), and send them, like the healed man, home to tell "how great things the Lord hath done" (Mar 5:19).
roots_summary: Greek and Latin historia → Old French estorie → English story → library story time → 2010s YouTube and c. 2020 TikTok: storytime, the anecdote video.
roots_lines: Greek historia — inquiry, an account; Latin historia
Old French estorie → Middle English storie, a narrative
Early 20th c.: story time in libraries and schools
2010s YouTube: STORYTIME videos, often over makeup or food
c. 2020 TikTok: multi-part storytimes
usage: "Storytime: the day my little brother locked us all out of the house."
Tell how great things the Lord hath done for thee (Mar 5:19).
Someone else’s secret is not your content (Pro 11:13).

etymology: Abbreviation of get ready with me, a video format that grew out of YouTube beauty channels in the early 2010s, where a creator does her makeup, hair, and outfit while chatting to the camera. TikTok and Instagram Reels made GRWM a staple c. 2020–2022, often combined with a storytime ("GRWM while I tell you about my worst date") and very often with product promotion.
biblical_def: In current slang a GRWM is a video where the creator gets ready — skincare, makeup, hair, outfit — while talking to the viewer as if to a friend in the bathroom. Many girls watch them every morning; many make them. Some are chatty and harmless; most are also a shop window. The Christian observation: Scripture has a get-ready-with-me, and it starts before the mirror. "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up" (Psa 5:3). Paul names the real outfit: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof" (Rom 13:14). Peter does not forbid care for appearance, but he weighs it: "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel" (1Pe 3:3), but "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4). The GRWM’s deeper trouble is the camera. Getting ready used to be private; now it is a performance, and Christ warned about doing even good things "before men, to be seen of them" (Mat 6:1). A girl who watches thirty GRWMs a week learns that her morning is content and that her face needs eleven products before it can be seen. A father tells his daughter: get ready well — clean, neat, glad to be a girl — and get ready first with Christ, in the Word and on your knees. The adorning He sees lasts longer than any routine.
webster_summary: Gen-Z abbreviation (YouTube 2010s, TikTok c. 2020–present) for a chatty get-ready-with-me video — a morning routine turned performance, which Scripture would begin with prayer and the putting on of Christ.
webster_full: GRWM, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, 2010s–present; YouTube and TikTok) Get ready with me: a video in which the creator does skincare, makeup, hair, and outfit while talking to the viewer. "GRWM for my first day of junior year."
Often combined: GRWM + storytime, GRWM for church, GRWM for a date; frequently carries paid product placement.
Older relatives: the beauty column, the department-store makeover, the older sister’s vanity table — private, or at least offline.

Webster (1828), root word ready: “READY, adjective red'y. […] 1. Quick; prompt; not hesitating; as ready wit; a ready consent. 2. Quick to receive or comprehend; not slow or dull; as a ready apprehension. 3. Quick in action or execution; dextrous; as an artist ready in his business; a ready writer. Psalms 45:1. 4. Prompt; not delayed present in hand.”
Decode for parents: count the products named in your daughter’s favourite GRWM; then ask who paid for the mention.
scriptures: My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: GRWM turns the private morning into a public performance and a sales floor, teaching girls that the face needs a routine before it may be seen.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with getting ready. Scripture has its own grooming scenes — Ruth washing and anointing herself before going down to Boaz, Esther’s months of preparation — and a girl who takes care with her appearance honours the people she will meet. Many GRWMs are simply a friendly voice in the morning.

The format changes two things. It makes the morning a stage — "before men, to be seen of them" (Mat 6:1) — and it makes the stage a shop: every serum is a sponsor, every outfit a link. A girl raised on it learns that being seen requires a routine, and the routine requires buying. Peter’s weighing still holds: the outward adorning is not to be the adorning (1Pe 3:3). Teach your daughter to get ready with the Lord first (Psa 5:3), to keep the mirror in its place, and to put on Christ (Rom 13:14) before anything else.
roots_summary: Old English ræde (prepared) → ready → 2010s YouTube: get ready with me → c. 2020 TikTok: GRWM.
roots_lines: Old English ræde — prepared, prompt; English ready
Get ready — to prepare oneself, especially to go out
Early 2010s YouTube beauty channels: get ready with me
c. 2020–2022 TikTok and Reels: GRWM, often with a storytime
Now: a daily genre and a major advertising channel
usage: "GRWM for youth group, and I’m telling you what happened at camp."
Get ready with the Lord first: in the morning will I direct my prayer (Psa 5:3).
Put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 13:14).

etymology: Korean meokbang (romanized mukbang), a blend of meokda (to eat) and bangsong (broadcast). The format arose on the Korean live-streaming site AfreecaTV c. 2009–2010: a host eats large amounts of food on camera while chatting with viewers, who send paid gifts. It spread worldwide on YouTube in the mid-2010s, with English-speaking creators eating enormous platters, and on TikTok in short clips, often with close microphones on the chewing (ASMR mukbang).
biblical_def: In current slang a mukbang is an eating broadcast: a host sits before a mountain of noodles, fried chicken, or seafood and eats it on camera, chatting and chewing into a close microphone, while thousands watch. Some viewers say it eases loneliness at mealtimes; some watch to eat vicariously while dieting; some watch for the sheer spectacle of excess. The Christian observation: eating is good, and eating together is holy. The first church "did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart" (Act 2:46), and "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1Co 10:31). But the mukbang inverts the table. It is eating as performance and excess as content, and Scripture has hard words for both. "Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh" (Pro 23:20) — and here the riotous eating is the show. Paul wept over those "whose God is their belly" (Php 3:19). Proverbs counsels a man "given to appetite" to "put a knife to thy throat" (Pro 23:2) — that is, to rule the appetite before it rules him. There is also a quiet sadness in it: a child eating alone in his room, watching a stranger eat on a screen, is hungry for a table. A father tells his son: food is a gift, and a feast is a joy; but gluttony on a screen is still gluttony, and watching it is not company. Come and eat with us. The Lord sets a table for His people, and He means us to sit at it together.
webster_summary: Korean meokbang, eating broadcast (AfreecaTV c. 2010; YouTube and TikTok worldwide) — eating as performance and excess as content, set against the glad, shared table of the church.
webster_full: MUKBANG, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2015–present in English; Korean origin, c. 2010) A video or live stream in which the host eats a large quantity of food while talking to viewers. "I watched a mukbang of a guy eating twelve burgers."
Also muk-bang, meokbang; ASMR mukbang, with close microphones on the chewing; mukbanger, the host.
No older English sense. A grandparent’s nearest picture is the pie-eating contest at the county fair — once a year, and never for company.

Webster (1828), root word eat: “EAT, verb transitive preterit tense ate; participle passive eat or eaten. […] 1. To bite or chew and swallow, as food. Men eat flesh and vegetables. They shall make thee to eat grass as oxen. Daniel 4:25. 2. To corrode; to wear away; to separate parts of a thing gradually, as an animal by gnawing. We say a cancer eats the flesh.”
Decode for parents: if your child watches mukbangs during his own meals, ask whether he is lonely at the table, or eating alone.
scriptures: And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh:
Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)
And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite.
corruption_summary: The mukbang turns the shared table into a spectacle of one man’s appetite, offering lonely viewers the look of company and the thrill of excess.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture is a book of feasts — the Passover, the wedding at Cana, the five thousand on the grass, the supper of the Lamb. Food is meant for gratitude and fellowship, "with gladness and singleness of heart" (Act 2:46). The mukbang keeps the food and drops the rest. There is no host and guest, only a performer and an audience; no grace said, only a gift counter; and the larger and more reckless the meal, the bigger the numbers.

That economy rewards the very thing Proverbs warns against: "the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty" (Pro 23:21), and some hosts have spoken openly about what years of it did to their bodies. For viewers who struggle with food, it can feed disordered eating in either direction. And the loneliness under it is real. Teach your children that the remedy for an empty chair is a full table: bring them to yours, say grace, and eat "to the glory of God" (1Co 10:31).
roots_summary: Korean meokda (to eat) + bangsong (broadcast) → meokbang on AfreecaTV c. 2010 → YouTube mid-2010s → TikTok clips and ASMR mukbang.
roots_lines: Korean meokda — to eat
Korean bangsong — a broadcast
c. 2009–2010 AfreecaTV: hosts eat on camera for paid viewer gifts
Mid-2010s YouTube: English-speaking mukbangers and giant platters
c. 2020 TikTok: short clips and close-mic chewing
usage: "I can’t eat lunch without a mukbang on, it’s too quiet."
Eat with gladness and singleness of heart, together (Act 2:46).
Whether ye eat or drink, do all to the glory of God (1Co 10:31).

etymology: From stream, flowing water, through streaming media (continuous delivery of audio or video over the internet, 1990s). Gamers broadcasting live on Justin.tv (2007) and its offshoot Twitch (2011) became streamers; by the late 2010s the word covered anyone who broadcasts live online — gamers, chatters, musicians, "IRL" streamers walking city streets — paid by subscriptions, donations, and sponsors. YouTube Live and Kick (2022) compete for them. The older English streamer is a long, narrow flag or a paper ribbon at a party.
biblical_def: In current slang a streamer is someone who broadcasts himself live online, usually for hours: playing games, reacting to videos, chatting with a scrolling crowd, or walking through a city with a camera. The biggest streamers earn millions, and many boys say they want to be one. The Christian observation: broadcasting is not new to Christians. Christ told His disciples, "What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops" (Mat 10:27) — the housetop was the first live stream, and the gospel has used every new platform since. A young man with a camera and a voice can serve God with them. But the streamer’s life presses on three weak points. Time: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16), and a ten-hour stream, watched or made, spends a day. Appetite: "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing" (Ecc 1:8), and the format is built never to end. Approval: the donations, the chat, and the subscriber count make a man’s income hang on pleasing a crowd, and Paul said, "if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). The streamers who hold a boy’s attention also shape his speech and temper, so Paul’s charge to the young applies on camera: "be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity" (1Ti 4:12). A father tells his son: if you broadcast, broadcast as a servant of Christ, with your mouth clean and your hours counted; and if you watch, remember that the man on the screen is not your friend and his day is not your day.
webster_summary: Internet slang (Justin.tv 2007, Twitch 2011–present) for one who broadcasts live online — a housetop Christ can use, and a life that tests a young man’s hours, appetite, and need for approval.
webster_full: STREAMER, n. (Gen-Z slang usage, c. 2011–present; Twitch and YouTube) One who broadcasts himself live online, usually at length, for an audience that chats and pays. "He wants to be a streamer when he grows up."
Stream, v.i., to broadcast live; going live; IRL streamer, one who streams everyday life outdoors; chat, the live audience; subs and donos, paid support.
Older senses: a long, narrow flag or pennant; a paper ribbon hung for a party; a ray of light shooting across the sky.

Webster (1828), root word streamer: “STREAMER, noun An ensign or flag; a pennon extended or flowing in the wind; a poetic use of the word. Brave Rupert from afar appears, whose waving streamers the glad general knows.”
Decode for parents: find out which streamers your son watches and for how many hours; they may be the most-heard adult voices in his week.
scriptures: What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops.
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
All things are full of labour; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
corruption_summary: The streamer life makes hours of self-broadcast a career and a crowd’s approval a paycheck, pressing on a young man’s time, appetite, and fear of man.
corruption_paragraphs: Christians should not be afraid of the camera. The gospel went from the housetops (Mat 10:27) to the printing press to the radio, and faithful men stream sermons and catechism classes every Lord’s Day. A boy who can speak clearly and hold an audience has a gift that can serve the church, and the platforms are mission fields like any other.

But the streaming economy rewards what Scripture warns against. It pays for hours, so time is spent without being redeemed (Eph 5:16). It pays for reaction, so the loudest temper and the crudest joke draw the biggest chat. And it pays by the crowd’s favour, minute by minute, which is the fear of man turned into an income: "if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). Teach your sons to count their hours, choose their voices, and if they ever broadcast, to be "an example of the believers, in word" (1Ti 4:12).
roots_summary: Old English stream (flowing water) → streamer, a flowing pennant → 1990s streaming media → 2007–2011 Justin.tv and Twitch: streamer, one who broadcasts live.
roots_lines: Old English stream — a current, flowing water
Middle English stremer — a long, flowing flag or pennant
1990s: streaming audio and video over the internet
2007 Justin.tv; 2011 Twitch: live-broadcasting gamers called streamers
2020s: streamers on Twitch, YouTube, and Kick; IRL and chatting streams
usage: "I watched his stream from after school till midnight."
Preach upon the housetops; a camera can serve Christ (Mat 10:27).
Redeem the time, on camera and off (Eph 5:16).

etymology: From rage and bait, on the pattern of clickbait. Used on forums and Twitter in the 2010s for posts made to anger readers into replying, it became common on TikTok and X c. 2022–2024, as platforms paid creators by engagement and outrage proved the cheapest way to earn it. Oxford University Press named rage bait its word of the year for 2025.
biblical_def: In current slang rage bait is content made to make you angry so that you will comment, share, and argue: the deliberately wrong recipe, the insulting opinion, the staged public scene. Anger is engagement, engagement is money, and the bait works whether you agree or not. The Christian observation: Proverbs described this trade three thousand years ago. "As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife" (Pro 26:21). The rage-baiter is that man with a ring light. Scripture’s first counsel is for the one tempted to bite: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:19–20). The angry comment you are itching to type is the fuel the post was built to burn. "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out" (Pro 26:20) — the surest answer to rage bait is to give it no wood. When an answer is needed, "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Pro 15:1). And for the one tempted to make it, the verdict is plain: stirring up strife for profit is selling your neighbour’s sin back to him. Christ was the opposite of rage bait: "when he was reviled, reviled not again" (1Pe 2:23). A father tells his son: when a post makes you furious, put the phone down; that fury is what they are harvesting. Be angry at real evil and say so plainly, but never let a stranger farm your temper for cash.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (2010s; mainstream c. 2022–present; Oxford word of the year 2025) for content built to provoke anger for engagement — the contentious man’s coals, which Scripture says to starve of wood.
webster_full: RAGE BAIT, n. (Gen-Z slang, 2010s–present; on the pattern of clickbait) Online content made deliberately to provoke anger so that viewers will comment, share, and argue. "Don’t reply to that, it’s rage bait."
Rage-bait, v.t., to provoke so; rage-baiter, one who does it; rage farming, the same practised as a business.
Older relatives: the tabloid headline, the provocateur, the uncle who "stirs the pot" at a family dinner.

Webster (1828), root word rage: “RAGE, noun […] 1. Violent anger accompanied with furious words, gestures or agitation; anger excited to fury. Passion sometimes rises to rage Torment and loud lament and furious rage 2. Vehemence or violent exacerbation of any thing painful; as the rage of pain; the rage of a fever; the rage of hunger or thirst. 3. Fury;”
Decode for parents: if your teen is angry after scrolling, someone probably meant him to be; teach him to notice the hook.
scriptures: As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
corruption_summary: Rage bait sells anger as engagement, paying the contentious man to kindle strife and harvesting the wrath of every viewer who takes the hook.
corruption_paragraphs: The business is simple and old. Find what makes people furious, say it as foolishly or as cruelly as possible, and let them do the rest. Proverbs named the man who does it: "a contentious man to kindle strife" (Pro 26:21). What is new is the scale and the payment. Platforms reward comments, and nothing generates comments like outrage, so a generation has learned that the fastest route to an audience is to make one furious.

The viewer is not innocent either. Every furious reply, quote, and stitch is wood for the fire, and "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out" (Pro 26:20). "The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20). Teach your children to recognise the hook, to scroll past, and to save their anger for real wrongs, answered with soft words and plain truth (Pro 15:1). And teach them never to bait anyone; the strife a man kindles for profit he will answer for.
roots_summary: Latin rabies (madness) → Old French rage + Old Norse beita (to make bite) → 2010s rage bait → 2025 Oxford word of the year.
roots_lines: Latin rabies — madness, fury; Old French rage
Old Norse beita — to cause to bite; English bait, a lure
c. 2006: clickbait and the economics of attention
2010s forums and Twitter: rage bait, posts made to anger
c. 2022–2025: engagement payouts; Oxford word of the year 2025
usage: "She posted that just to make everyone mad. Pure rage bait."
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out (Pro 26:20).
A soft answer turneth away wrath (Pro 15:1).

etymology: From click and bait. Attested by 2006 in blogs complaining of headlines written to lure clicks; the style took over viral news sites and YouTube in the early 2010s ("You won’t believe what happens next," the shocked-face thumbnail, the red arrow), and the major dictionaries entered the word during that decade. Gen Z uses it for any title or thumbnail that over-promises.
biblical_def: In current slang clickbait is a headline, title, or thumbnail written to lure a click with a promise the content will not keep: "Doctors HATE this one trick," a red arrow, a shocked face, "(GONE WRONG)." Teens call it out instantly and click anyway. The Christian observation: clickbait is a false weight. "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Pro 11:1). A headline is a measure — it tells you what you are buying with your time — and a headline that lies is a short measure. Its method is the tempter’s: "every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed" (Jas 1:14); the bait works by finding the curiosity, fear, or greed already in us. Paul describes men who "by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple" (Rom 16:18). And the payoff never matches the bait: "Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel" (Pro 20:17) — every child who has finished a clickbait video knows that taste. Christ’s rule for speech governs titles too: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). A father tells his son: if you ever make videos, title them honestly, even if fewer people click; and when a thumbnail screams at you, ask what it wants from you before you give it your time. The gospel is the one headline that under-promises: eye hath not seen what God has prepared for them that love Him (1Co 2:9).
webster_summary: Internet slang (c. 2006; mainstream 2010s–present) for a misleading headline or thumbnail built to lure clicks — a false weight in the market of attention, which God calls abomination.
webster_full: CLICKBAIT, n. (Gen-Z slang usage, c. 2006–present) A headline, title, or thumbnail that lures clicks with a promise the content does not keep. "The title said he quit YouTube. Total clickbait."
Clickbaity, adj.; clickbait thumbnail, with arrows, circles, and shocked faces; not clickbait, a title’s protest that it is honest (often untrue).
Older relatives: the sensational tabloid headline, the carnival barker, the bait-and-switch advertisement.

Webster (1828), root word lure: “LURE, noun 1. Something held out to call a hawk; hence, 2. Any enticement; that which invites by the prospect of advantage or pleasure; as the lures of beauty or of gain.”
Decode for parents: clickbait teaches children that exaggeration is normal; reward honest titles in their own schoolwork and posts.
scriptures: A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.
For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple.
Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
corruption_summary: Clickbait sells time by a false measure, luring the curious with promises the content will not keep and training a generation to accept exaggeration as normal.
corruption_paragraphs: Every market has had its cheats, and Scripture judges them by the scales: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD" (Pro 11:1). In the attention market the scale is the headline. It tells you what you will get for your minutes, and clickbait shortchanges you on purpose, because the click has already paid the seller. The method is enticement (Jas 1:14): it finds the itch already in us and scratches just enough to make us bite.

The deeper damage is to the conscience. Children raised on clickbait learn that everyone exaggerates, that "(GONE WRONG)" means nothing went wrong, and that honest speech is naive. Then they write their own titles the same way. "Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel" (Pro 20:17). Teach your children Christ’s rule, "Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37), for titles as well as promises, and show them that the Bible’s greatest news is never oversold.
roots_summary: Imitative English click + Old Norse beita (bait) → c. 2006 clickbait, headlines that lure clicks → 2010s YouTube thumbnails → any over-promising title.
roots_lines: Imitative English click — a small sharp sound; later, to press a mouse button
Old Norse beita — to cause to bite; English bait, food on a hook
c. 2006: clickbait in blogs criticising lure headlines
Early 2010s: viral-news headlines and YouTube thumbnails
Now: any title or thumbnail that over-promises
usage: "It said he was leaving and he was just going on vacation. Clickbait."
A just weight is the Lord’s delight, in headlines too (Pro 11:1).
Bread of deceit is sweet, then gravel (Pro 20:17).

etymology: A Twitter and TikTok construction of c. 2019–2020, drawn from Black Twitter usage: "Not me" followed by an -ing verb ("not me crying at a dog-food commercial") confesses something embarrassing one has just done while pretending to deny it. The pretended denial is the joke; everyone hears it as an admission. The same frame is used of others: "not him thinking he could beat me," "not the teacher calling on me."
biblical_def: In current slang not me plus an -ing verb is a confession dressed as a denial: "not me eating the whole pizza," "not me forgetting my own birthday." The speaker admits something embarrassing and laughs at herself in the same breath. The Christian observation: this little idiom is healthier than most. It is self-mockery without self-pity, and the ability to laugh at your own foolishness is a mercy; there is "a time to laugh" (Ecc 3:4). But it also preserves, in a joke, the oldest human reflex: to answer "not me." Adam blamed the woman, the woman blamed the serpent, and the reflex has run in the family ever since. Scripture answers it twice over. When David hid his sin, Nathan said, "Thou art the man" (2Sa 12:7). When Jesus said one of the Twelve would betray Him, the disciples did not say "not me"; they "began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?" (Mat 26:22). That is the posture of a heart under grace: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Pro 28:13). And the confession has a sure answer: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1Jn 1:9). A father tells his children: keep laughing at the small things you get wrong; it will keep you humble. And when the thing is not small, drop the joke and say it plainly — to God and to whoever you wronged. The only thing better than a funny confession is a forgiven one.
webster_summary: Gen-Z construction (Twitter / TikTok c. 2019–present) for a self-mocking confession in the shape of a denial — a humble laugh that Scripture would carry all the way to "Lord, is it I?"
webster_full: NOT ME, phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2019–present; Twitter and TikTok) Followed by an -ing verb, a playful confession of something embarrassing one has just done, framed as a mock denial. "Not me crying at a commercial for dog food."
Extended to others: "not him thinking he could beat me," "not the teacher calling on me the one day I didn’t read." Always heard as an admission or an exclamation, never a real denial.
Older sense: the plain denial, "Not me!" — every child’s first answer to "Who broke this?"

Webster (1828), root word confess: “CONFESS', verb transitive […] 1. To own, acknowledge or avow, as a crime, a fault, a charge, a debt, or something that is against one's interest, or reputation. Human faults with human grief confess I confess the argument against me is good and not easily refuted. let us frankly confess our sins.”
Decode for parents: a harmless habit of laughing at oneself; use it to teach the difference between a funny confession and a real one.
scriptures: And they were exceeding sorrowful, and began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?
And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
corruption_summary: Not me is a healthy self-mockery that keeps, in a joke, the oldest human reflex of denial, which Scripture turns around into honest confession.
corruption_paragraphs: There is grace in a generation that can laugh at itself. "Not me tripping up the stairs in front of the whole class" is humility in miniature: the speaker owns the foolishness and invites others to laugh with her. Pride cannot do that. A child who can say it is better prepared than many adults for the harder confessions Scripture asks of us (Pro 28:13).

But the shape of the joke is the shape of the fall. The first sinners answered God’s question by pointing elsewhere, and their children have done the same ever since. The gospel teaches the reverse sentence. Nathan’s "Thou art the man" (2Sa 12:7) broke David into Psalm 51, and the disciples’ "Lord, is it I?" (Mat 26:22) is the question of men who know their own hearts. Teach your children to keep the laugh for small things and to use plain words for sin, because "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1Jn 1:9).
roots_summary: Middle English not (from nought) + me → the child’s denial, "Not me!" → c. 2019 Black Twitter and TikTok: not me + -ing, the mock-denial confession.
roots_lines: Middle English not, from Old English nawiht — nothing, not at all
Old English me — the first person, objective case
Everyday English: "Not me!" as a plain denial
c. 2019–2020 Black Twitter, then TikTok: not me + -ing as playful confession
Now: not him, not the teacher — the same frame for others
usage: "Not me studying the wrong chapter for the whole weekend."
The disciples did not say not me; they said, Lord, is it I? (Mat 26:22).
Whoso confesseth and forsaketh shall have mercy (Pro 28:13).
